Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘probing pole and shadow grass.’ Linji's own record places the phrase third in his fourfold classification of a shout, after the Diamond King's jeweled sword and the crouching golden-haired lion and before a shout that does not function as a shout. Later records preserve it as a public category: masters are asked ‘what is a shout like probing pole and shadow grass?’ Recorded answers include ‘I have tested what bones you have’ (驗得你骨出) and ‘I know whether you are a dragon or a snake’ (知你是龍是蛇). A later comment calls a particular conversational move ‘also probing pole and shadow grass,’ and another record says a staff may function this way. These attested predicates place the ordinary images in encounters as a named testing gambit. The sources quoted here retain the compound and do not separately define the pole and the grass.
Senses.Note: 251 raw hits in 102 allowlist texts. Cross-checked all four Linji shout classifications. The simplified-graph variant (寻竿影草) was not adopted; the traditional probing-pole form (探竿影草) is the headword and dominant form. One corpus-wide sense is sufficient.
